title: async and await
summary: Write non-blocking code with async methods, Task and await, run work concurrently with Task.WhenAll, call HTTP APIs with HttpClient and cancel with CancellationToken.
introduction: Waiting is the most common thing programs do: for a web response, a database query, a file on a slow disk. A thread that blocks while waiting wastes a core on a server and freezes the window in a desktop app. C#'s async and await let you write code that reads like ordinary sequential code but gives the thread back while waiting. This lesson explains what a Task is, how await works, how to run several operations at once, how to call a web API with HttpClient, and how to cancel work that takes too long.
learningObjectives: Declare async methods that return Task and Task<T> and await them
Run independent operations concurrently with Task.WhenAll
Use HttpClient and CancellationToken in async code

blocks.text: A `Task` represents work that will finish in the future; `Task<T>` is work that will produce a `T`. Methods that return tasks are conventionally named with an `Async` suffix. Inside a method marked `async`, the `await` keyword pauses the method until the task completes *without blocking the thread*: the method returns to its caller and resumes later, right where it left off, with the result unwrapped. Top-level statements may use `await` directly.

blocks.content:
Putting the kettle on...
Your tea is ready

blocks.text: `Task.Delay(1000)` is an asynchronous one-second timer: unlike `Thread.Sleep`, it does not occupy a thread while waiting. The `async` modifier lets the compiler rewrite the method into a state machine, and `return` inside it provides the `T` of the `Task<T>`. The output order is exactly what sequential code would give; `await` only changes *how* the waiting happens.

rows: An async method with no result (the async equivalent of `void`)
An async method that produces a value
Hot paths where the result is usually already available; otherwise prefer `Task<T>`
Event handlers only; exceptions escape and nobody can await the method

blocks.text: Awaiting one task after another runs them one at a time. When operations do not depend on each other, start them all first and then `await Task.WhenAll(...)`, which completes when every task has finished and returns their results as an array. The program measures both approaches with a `Stopwatch`.

blocks.title: Output (timings are approximate)
blocks.content:
Sequential: tea done, toast done in about 4 s
Concurrent: tea done, toast done in about 2 s

blocks.text: The concurrency comes from overlapping *waits*, not from extra threads: both delays tick at the same time without occupying any thread. For CPU-heavy work (image processing, big calculations) use `Task.Run` to move it to a thread-pool thread so that the caller stays responsive.

The most common real use of `await` is I/O. `HttpClient` sends HTTP requests, and all its methods are asynchronous. `GetAsync` returns the response with its status and headers; `ReadAsStringAsync` downloads the body. One `HttpClient` should be created once and reused; the `using` declaration disposes it when the program ends.

For JSON APIs, `http.GetFromJsonAsync<T>(url)` from the `System.Net.Http.Json` namespace downloads and deserialises the body into your own record type in one awaited call; the [files and JSON lesson](/tutorials/csharp/files-json) covers the serializer it uses.

An exception thrown inside an async method is stored in its task and rethrown when the task is awaited, so an ordinary `try`/`catch` around an `await` works. Long operations should accept a `CancellationToken` and pass it to every async call they make; when the source is cancelled, those calls throw `OperationCanceledException` and the work stops at the next await.

Once a method awaits, its callers should await it too, all the way up to the entry point. Mixing in blocking calls defeats the purpose and can deadlock, which is the subject of the warning below. In ASP.NET Core and most libraries every I/O API already has an async version; use it, and let the `Async` suffix remind you to `await`.

blocks.title: Never block on a task with .Result or .Wait()
blocks.text: `string s = GetAsync().Result;` blocks the current thread until the task finishes. In UI apps and older ASP.NET it deadlocks, because the task needs that very thread to resume on; everywhere else it wastes a thread and wraps exceptions in an `AggregateException`. Make the calling method `async` and `await` instead. Likewise avoid `async void` (except for event handlers): its exceptions cannot be caught by the caller and nobody can await it.

questions.question: What does await do when the task it is waiting for has not finished yet?
questions.explanation: `await` suspends the async method and returns control to the caller; the method resumes when the task completes. No thread is blocked and no new thread is created for the wait.
options: Blocks the current thread until the task finishes
Returns control to the caller and resumes the method when the task completes
Creates a new thread to run the task

questions.question: Task.WhenAll starts the given tasks one after another and returns when the last one finishes.
questions.explanation: The tasks are already running when they are passed in; `WhenAll` only produces a task that completes once all of them have completed, so their waits overlap.
